note: 50 questions, all one level. Built for surprise while staying guessable. Every citation points at a source retrieved during research.

questions.prompt: How many people died in conflicts in 2024?
questions.whyCorrect: 48,384 documented deaths — one life lost every 12 minutes, and 40% more than in 2023.
questions.action: Work out how many deaths that is per day.

questions.prompt: Conflict deaths in 2024 compared with 2023:
questions.whyCorrect: Rose 40% — the sharpest recent deterioration in any Goal 16 indicator.
questions.action: Name the conflicts that escalated in 2024.

questions.prompt: One conflict death occurs, on average, every:
questions.whyCorrect: Every 12 minutes. Nearly 50,000 deaths a year, spread evenly, is roughly five people every hour of every day.
whyWrong: Far too infrequent for 48,384 deaths a year.
questions.action: Divide the minutes in a year by 48,384.

questions.prompt: Children killed in conflict in 2023-2024 rose by how much over the previous two years?
questions.whyCorrect: 337% — more than a fourfold increase. Children are being killed in conflict at rates without recent precedent.
questions.action: Ask why civilian deaths rise in urban warfare.

questions.prompt: Women killed in conflict in 2023-2024 rose by:
questions.whyCorrect: 258% — a more than threefold rise, alongside the 337% increase for children. Conflict is increasingly hitting civilians.
questions.action: Ask what protections civilians have under international law.

questions.prompt: How many people were forcibly displaced by the end of 2024?
questions.whyCorrect: 123.2 million — more than the population of Japan, forced from home by conflict and persecution.
questions.action: Find a country with about 123 million people.

questions.prompt: The global homicide rate fell from 5.9 per 100,000 in 2015 to:
questions.whyCorrect: 5.2 per 100,000 by 2023 — a real decline, but on track for only a 25% reduction by 2030 against a 50% target.
questions.action: Look up the homicide rate in your country.

questions.prompt: The homicide reduction target for 2030 is 50%. Current projections reach:
questions.whyCorrect: 25% — half the target. Genuine progress, at half the pace the world committed to.
whyWrong: That's the target, not the projection.
questions.action: Ask what has driven homicide rates down since 2015.

questions.prompt: What share of homicide victims are men?
questions.whyCorrect: 80% — homicide is overwhelmingly a risk to men, mostly young men, mostly outside the home.
questions.action: Ask why young men are most at risk of homicide.

questions.prompt: How many women were killed by partners or family members in 2023?
questions.whyCorrect: About 51,000 — roughly 140 women a day, killed by someone they knew. For women, the most dangerous place is often home.
questions.action: Divide 51,000 by 365.

questions.prompt: Male homicide fell 14% since 2015. Female homicide fell:
questions.whyCorrect: Only 5%. Public violence is falling much faster than violence inside the home, which policing reaches less easily.
whyWrong: The decline for women was much smaller.
questions.action: Ask why domestic violence is harder to reduce.

questions.prompt: Detected human trafficking victims rose how much compared with 2020?
questions.whyCorrect: 43% more detected victims than in 2020, and 25% more than pre-pandemic — partly better detection, partly more trafficking.
questions.action: Ask what makes trafficking hard to detect.

questions.prompt: Children are what share of all detected trafficking victims?
questions.whyCorrect: 38% — more than a third, and up 31% since 2019. Children are the fastest-growing group of trafficking victims.
questions.action: Look up what trafficking actually involves.

questions.prompt: What share of trafficked girls are exploited sexually?
questions.whyCorrect: 60% of trafficked girls, while 45% of trafficked boys are exploited for forced labour. Traffickers target children differently by gender.
questions.action: Look up who to contact about suspected trafficking.

questions.prompt: What share of trafficked boys are exploited for forced labour?
questions.whyCorrect: 45% — compared with 60% of girls trafficked for sexual exploitation. Both patterns are severe and distinct.
whyWrong: Too high — the figure is under half.
questions.action: Ask what industries forced labour appears in.

questions.prompt: How many people are in prison worldwide?
questions.whyCorrect: 11.7 million — and 3.7 million of them have never been sentenced for anything.
questions.action: Look up your country's prison population.

questions.prompt: How many prisoners have never been sentenced?
questions.whyCorrect: 3.7 million — 31% of all prisoners are held before trial, presumed innocent under law but locked up in fact.
questions.action: Ask how long someone can be held before trial where you live.

questions.prompt: Pretrial detention as a share of prisoners went from 29% in 2015 to:
questions.whyCorrect: 31% — it got slightly worse. Court backlogs mean more people wait in cells for trials that may take years.
whyWrong: Too high — it is just under a third.
The share rose rather than fell.
questions.action: Ask what 'innocent until proven guilty' means in practice.

questions.prompt: What share of unsentenced detainees are men?
questions.whyCorrect: 94% men, 6% women — mirroring the wider pattern where men are most involved in and most affected by public violence and policing.
questions.action: Ask why prison populations are so heavily male.

questions.prompt: How many human rights defenders were killed in 2024?
questions.whyCorrect: 502 killings across 44 countries, plus 123 disappearances in 37 countries. Defending rights is measurably dangerous work.
questions.action: Look up what a human rights defender does.

questions.prompt: How many journalists were killed in 2024?
questions.whyCorrect: 82 — an 11% increase, with over 60% killed in conflict zones. Reporting from a war is now among the deadliest jobs there is.
questions.action: Ask why a country would want to silence journalists.

questions.prompt: What share of journalist killings happened in conflict zones?
questions.whyCorrect: Over 60% — but that means nearly 40% were killed outside any war, often for investigating corruption or crime.
whyWrong: Conflict zones account for the majority.
questions.action: Look up a journalist killed for an investigation.

questions.prompt: How many countries have access-to-information laws?
questions.whyCorrect: 140 countries — up from just 14 in 1990. A tenfold rise in the legal right to ask governments what they are doing.
questions.action: Find out how to request public information in your country.

questions.prompt: In 1990, how many countries had access-to-information laws?
questions.whyCorrect: Just 14. The right to know what your government does is a remarkably recent legal invention in most of the world.
questions.action: Ask what a government could hide before such laws.

questions.prompt: How many countries have fully compliant national human rights institutions?
questions.whyCorrect: 89, up from 70 in 2015. These bodies investigate abuses independently of the government that funds them.
questions.action: Find out if your country has one.

questions.prompt: Government budget deviation — the gap between planned and actual spending — improved from 12.6% in 2020 to:
questions.whyCorrect: 9.6% by 2023. Governments are spending closer to what they publicly promised — a quiet but real accountability gain.
whyWrong: The figure improved rather than worsened.
questions.action: Ask why a government might not spend what it budgeted.

questions.prompt: Conflict deaths rose 40% while homicide fell. Together this suggests:
options: Everyday violence is declining while organised armed conflict is intensifying
questions.whyCorrect: Two different trends: policing and development are reducing everyday killings, while wars are getting deadlier.
whyWrong: The homicide rate fell from 5.9 to 5.2.
questions.action: Ask why these two trends move independently.

questions.prompt: 31% of prisoners being unsentenced matters because:
options: People presumed innocent lose jobs, homes and family ties while waiting for trial
questions.whyCorrect: Pretrial detention punishes before any verdict — and those who cannot afford bail or a lawyer are the ones who wait longest.
whyWrong: By law they are presumed innocent.
questions.action: Ask what happens to someone's job after six months in detention.

questions.prompt: The 337% rise in children killed in conflict mainly reflects:
options: Fighting moving into densely populated civilian areas
questions.whyCorrect: When conflicts are fought in cities and camps, civilians — especially children — make up a far larger share of the casualties.
whyWrong: Population change cannot explain a fourfold rise.
The increase reflects a real change in casualties.
questions.action: Ask what makes urban warfare different for civilians.

questions.prompt: 51,000 women killed by partners or family means roughly:
questions.whyCorrect: About 140 women every day, killed by someone who knew them. It's the single largest category of gender-based lethal violence.
questions.action: Find out what support services exist near you.

questions.prompt: Access-to-information laws going from 14 to 140 countries shows:
options: Transparency has become a global legal norm in one generation
questions.whyCorrect: A tenfold rise in 35 years. The idea that citizens can demand government records went from rare to standard.
whyWrong: The legal trend is strongly toward openness.
questions.action: Try finding your local government's spending records.

questions.prompt: 123.2 million forcibly displaced people compares with 2015 as:
options: Far higher — displacement has risen every year
questions.whyCorrect: Displacement has risen essentially every year of the SDG period, driven by conflicts whose death toll rose 40% in 2024 alone.
questions.action: Ask how long the average refugee stays displaced.

questions.prompt: Homicide falling 14% for men but 5% for women shows:
options: Violence in public spaces is easier to reduce than violence at home
questions.whyCorrect: Street policing, lighting and youth programmes cut public violence. Killings inside families need entirely different interventions.
whyWrong: Their rate fell far less than men's.
questions.action: Ask what policy reduces violence inside homes.

questions.prompt: National human rights institutions rising from 70 to 89 countries means:
options: More countries have independent bodies that can investigate their own government
questions.whyCorrect: A fully compliant institution can investigate a government that funds it — which is precisely why building one is politically difficult.
whyWrong: The number of compliant institutions rose.
It's a tracked SDG indicator with clear criteria.
questions.action: Look up what makes such an institution 'compliant'.

questions.prompt: Trafficking detections rising 43% since 2020 could mean:
options: Either more trafficking, better detection, or both
questions.whyCorrect: Detection figures measure what authorities find, not what exists. Rising numbers can mean a worse problem or better policing — usually both.
whyWrong: Detection capacity also improved over this period.
questions.action: Ask why 'detected' and 'actual' are different numbers.

questions.prompt: Human rights defenders were killed across how many countries in 2024?
questions.whyCorrect: 44 countries recorded killings, and 37 recorded disappearances. This is not confined to a handful of states.
questions.action: Ask what causes defenders are usually working on.

questions.prompt: The homicide rate of 5.2 per 100,000 means, in a city of a million:
questions.whyCorrect: About 52 a year on the global average — though rates vary more than tenfold between countries and neighbourhoods.
questions.action: Multiply 5.2 by ten for a per-million figure.

questions.prompt: Journalist killings rising 11% while over 60% occur in conflict zones suggests:
options: Escalating conflicts are the main driver, but non-conflict killings persist
questions.whyCorrect: The 40% rise in conflict deaths drags journalist deaths up with it — while nearly 40% still die investigating stories in peacetime.
questions.action: Look up how journalists protect themselves in conflict.

questions.prompt: Why does Goal 16 group peace, justice and institutions together?
options: Without functioning courts and honest institutions, peace and rights cannot be enforced
questions.whyCorrect: Rights without courts are words on paper. Goal 16 treats institutions as the machinery that makes peace and justice real.
whyWrong: The grouping reflects function, not naming.
questions.action: Ask what happens to a right nobody can enforce.

questions.prompt: Budget deviation improving from 12.6% to 9.6% means governments are:
options: Spending closer to what they publicly promised
questions.whyCorrect: A smaller gap between the published budget and actual spending means the public budget is a more honest description of what happens.
whyWrong: It measures accuracy, not total spending.
It indicates more accountability, not less.
questions.action: Ask why matching your budget is a sign of good management.

questions.prompt: 38% of trafficking victims being children, up 31% since 2019, is alarming because:
options: Children are the least able to escape or report it
Children are trafficked less than adults
questions.whyCorrect: Children have the least power to leave, complain or be believed — and they are the fastest-growing share of detected victims.
questions.action: Look up the warning signs of child trafficking.

questions.prompt: 80% of homicide victims are men, but 51,000 women are killed by family. Together this means:
options: Men face more homicide overall; women face more homicide from people they know
questions.whyCorrect: The risk profile differs completely by gender — which is why one policy cannot address both patterns.
whyWrong: 51,000 women were killed by partners or family in 2023.
questions.action: Ask what different policies each pattern needs.

questions.prompt: 48,384 conflict deaths in 2024 is what compared with the 2023 figure?
questions.whyCorrect: About 40% higher — meaning roughly 14,000 additional deaths in a single year of escalation.
questions.action: Calculate what 2023's total would have been.

questions.prompt: Which Goal 16 indicator has improved most clearly?
questions.whyCorrect: A tenfold rise in transparency laws since 1990. Conflict deaths rose 40% and pretrial detention worsened from 29% to 31%.
questions.action: Find one thing your government publishes that it once wouldn't have.

questions.prompt: Homicide falling 25% by 2030 instead of the 50% target means:
options: Real progress at half the committed pace
questions.whyCorrect: A quarter fewer killings is thousands of lives saved — and still only half of what governments agreed to deliver.
whyWrong: The projection falls short of the target.
questions.action: Ask what would double the rate of improvement.

questions.prompt: Corruption and weak institutions matter for the other 16 goals because:
options: Money meant for schools, clinics and water disappears before it arrives
questions.whyCorrect: Every other goal runs on public money and public rules. That's why budget accuracy and information laws are tracked as SDG indicators.
whyWrong: Institutional quality shapes delivery of every goal.
It affects all public spending, not just justice.
questions.action: Trace how funding reaches your school.

questions.prompt: 94% of unsentenced detainees being men reflects:
options: The same gender pattern seen in homicide and arrests generally
questions.whyCorrect: Men are 80% of homicide victims and the overwhelming majority of those arrested and detained — a consistent global pattern.
whyWrong: The figure is consistent with other justice statistics.
questions.action: Ask why criminal justice systems are so male-dominated.

questions.prompt: 502 defenders killed and 123 disappeared in 2024 shows that:
options: Speaking up against powerful interests carries lethal risk in dozens of countries
questions.whyCorrect: Across 44 countries, people were killed for defending land, labour, environmental or human rights. Disappearance is often used to intimidate others.
whyWrong: Each figure represents a person killed or missing.
questions.action: Look up a defender killed for protecting land or forest.

questions.prompt: The 40% rise in conflict deaths alongside 123.2 million displaced shows:
options: Conflict is both killing more people and uprooting more
questions.whyCorrect: The two move together — people flee the same violence that is killing civilians at rising rates.
whyWrong: Conflict is the primary driver of displacement.
questions.action: Ask what happens to a city's population during a war.

questions.prompt: The sharpest Goal 16 warning sign is:
options: A 337% rise in children killed in conflict
questions.whyCorrect: Children killed in conflict more than quadrupled in two years — the fastest deterioration of any indicator in the goal.
whyWrong: That is a major success, up from 14 in 1990.
questions.action: Look up what the Geneva Conventions say about children.
